entities.name: ABC Records
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
ABC Records (American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres Records), founded in 1955 by ABC and Paramount Theatres as a joint record label venture, was a significant American record label from the late 1950s through the 1970s — home to Ray Charles (who moved from Atlantic Records to ABC in 1959), B.B. King, Jim Croce, Steely Dan, and various other major artists before its 1979 acquisition by MCA Records, which absorbed ABC-Dunhill (its parent by then) into what became Universal Music Group.

ABC Records' most historically significant achievement was the 1959 signing of Ray Charles from Atlantic Records — a landmark moment that gave Charles not only a significant signing bonus but, crucially, ownership of his masters and distribution control unprecedented for Black artists of the era. This contractual achievement, negotiated by Charles's manager, made Ray Charles among the first Black American artists to own his recordings — a precedent that would influence subsequent artist-label negotiations. Charles's ABC recordings include the country-crossing Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music (1962, the year's best-selling album), demonstrating the cross-genre appeal that Atlantic had recognized but ABC fully commercial developed.

ABC-Dunhill (formed through ABC's acquisition of Dunhill Records) was home to Steely Dan and other major 1970s acts. The label's 1979 MCA acquisition ended its independent existence, though its back catalog (including Ray Charles's defining ABC albums) remains in circulation. ABC Records' significance rests primarily on the Ray Charles master ownership precedent, which influenced the broader evolution of artist rights in the American recording industry.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: ABC Records — primarily historically significant for Ray Charles's master ownership precedent (1959) influencing artist rights evolution, and for his crossover hit Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music — is a label whose importance is larger than its commercial lifespan suggests due to the Ray Charles rights innovation.
